text:
Why Primary Schools Should Keep Teaching Joined Handwriting

Every few years a headline declares that handwriting is finished. Keyboards are faster, the argument goes, and children will spend their adult lives tapping screens, so why should a seven year old spend precious classroom time learning to loop an l or link an e to an r? It is a tempting line of reasoning, and it has persuaded some education systems to drop cursive from their curricula altogether. I think they have made a mistake. Primary schools should keep teaching joined handwriting, and they should teach it well, with short daily practice in the early years and clear expectations by the time children are nine or ten. The case rests on what joined writing does for the developing brain, for fluency, for spelling, and for fairness between children. It also rests on something simpler, which is that a person who can write quickly and legibly by hand has a tool that never runs out of battery.

Let me begin by granting what the other side gets right. Typing is an essential skill, and no child should leave primary school unable to use a keyboard with reasonable confidence. Handwriting will never again be the only way most people produce text, and nobody sensible is asking schools to pretend otherwise. But the choice on offer is a false one. Schools do not have to pick between pens and keyboards any more than they have to pick between reading and arithmetic. Fifteen minutes of handwriting practice a day sits comfortably beside weekly typing lessons. The real question is narrower and more interesting. Given that children will learn to write by hand, should the hand they learn be joined or printed, and should it be taught deliberately or left to chance? On both counts I say joined, and deliberately.

Start with what happens inside a child's head. Researchers who study early literacy have found that the physical act of forming letters matters in ways that tapping a key does not. In a well known series of studies, the psychologist Karin James scanned the brains of young children who had not yet learned to read. Those who practised drawing letters by hand showed activity in the regions that adults use for reading. Those who typed the same letters, or traced over them, showed far less. A Norwegian study of students using electrodes found richer patterns of connectivity across the brain during handwriting than during typing. None of this proves that cursive in particular is magic, and honest researchers say the field is still young. But the direction of the evidence is consistent. Moving a pen through the shapes of letters seems to help the brain learn what those letters are, and a flowing script asks for more of that movement, not less.

Why joined rather than printed? Because of what a join does mechanically. When a child prints, every letter is a separate act. The pen lifts, travels, lands, and starts again. When a child joins, the hand moves through a whole word in one connected motion, and the word becomes a single pattern rather than a pile of parts. That has practical consequences. Speed is the obvious one, since a fluent joined hand is quicker than print for most writers once it has become automatic. But there is another benefit that teachers notice daily. Letters that children habitually confuse, such as b and d, are formed with different entry strokes in a joined script, and the movement itself becomes a reminder of which is which. Many specialists who work with dyslexic pupils recommend cursive for this reason, and while the research base here is thinner than anyone would like, the classroom experience is remarkably consistent.

Joined writing also seems to support spelling. When letter strings such as ing, tion, ough or ed are written as a single movement, they start to feel like units, and the hand remembers them even when the mind hesitates. Most of us have had the experience of being unsure how to spell a word until we write it down and see whether it looks and feels right. That is motor memory at work. A child who writes words as connected wholes builds that memory faster than one who assembles them letter by letter. I would not claim the evidence is conclusive. But primary teachers who use joined script from an early stage routinely report that their pupils' spelling is steadier, and there is a plausible mechanism to explain why.

The strongest argument, to my mind, is about cognitive load. A child has only so much working memory. If forming each letter still takes conscious effort, then less attention is left over for the things that make writing worth doing, which are choosing words, building sentences and holding an idea in mind long enough to finish it. The educational psychologist Steve Graham and others have shown repeatedly that children whose handwriting is slow or effortful write shorter and weaker compositions than their abilities deserve. Automatic handwriting frees the mind. And automaticity comes from practice with a system that is efficient enough to be worth practising. Printed letters can be automatic too, but they cap out at a lower speed. By the upper years of primary school, and certainly by secondary school, children who cannot write quickly by hand are at a real disadvantage. Many national examinations are still written by hand, often under time pressure. A fast, legible, joined hand is a quiet advantage that lasts for years.

There is also a question of fairness. Not every child grows up in a house with a laptop, a tablet and a parent who has time to teach good habits. Every child can be given a pencil and a piece of paper, and every school can teach them how to use it. If joined handwriting is dropped from the curriculum, it does not disappear. It becomes something that children from privileged homes pick up through private tutoring, calligraphy clubs and attentive parents, while others are left with an awkward, laboured scrawl. We have seen this pattern before with other skills that schools stopped teaching systematically. Whatever is left to the home favours those with the most resources. Handwriting is one of the few basic crafts where a school can give every child the same start at almost no cost.

The objections deserve straight answers. The first is time. The curriculum is crowded, and every minute spent on loops is a minute not spent on something else. But handwriting does not need to be a separate subject taking up whole afternoons. Short, frequent sessions of ten or fifteen minutes, tied to spelling and phonics, are far more effective than long ones, and they double as a calm start to the day. The second objection is that most adults do not join up anyway. They develop a personal hybrid of print and cursive. That is true, and it is not a point against teaching joins. It is how learning works. A driving instructor does not expect every pupil to drive exactly as taught for life, but the foundation shapes what comes after. A child taught a clear joined script can adapt it. A child taught nothing has nothing to adapt. The third objection is that cursive is old fashioned. Perhaps, but being able to read a grandparent's letter, an archive document or a note in a margin is not nothing, and neither is signing your own name with confidence.

None of this is an argument for the grim handwriting drills that some of us remember. Good teaching matters enormously. The best approaches begin with simple letters that already carry small exit strokes, so that joins feel like a natural extension rather than a new alphabet. They pay attention to posture, paper position and pencil grip, which prevent fatigue and bad habits. They teach children to join early, rather than printing for years and then asking them to unlearn it. They allow left handed children to angle their paper and adapt the slant without being scolded. They treat legibility and fluency as the goals, not perfect copperplate, and they let children develop personal style once the basics are secure. And they sit alongside regular keyboard instruction from around the age of seven or eight, so that no child is shortchanged on either skill. Done like this, joined handwriting is a modest, enjoyable part of the school day rather than a burden.

The debate is sometimes framed as tradition against progress, and that framing flatters the wrong side. Dropping joined handwriting is not a leap into the future. It is the removal of a cheap, effective tool that supports reading, spelling, speed and equality, in exchange for a small saving of classroom time. The evidence on brain development is encouraging if not yet complete, the practical benefits are visible in classrooms, and the costs are low. Children will live in a world of screens, and they should be taught to master them. They will also have moments when a pen is the only thing at hand and a fluent, legible line is what is needed. Primary schools should prepare them for both, and that means keeping the loop.
